submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole marks an indefinite quantity/extent phrase: it fires on 'a'/'an' where the model expects such a phrase's degree or amount word next ('a lot of', 'a few', 'a number of', 'a variety of', 'a wide range', 'a high standard', 'a good deal'), and on the degree modifier itself when it follows (wide, vast, broad, high, long, good, great, very, significant); its output direction promotes exactly those quantity heads (variety, array, range, multitude, slew, plethora, host, lot), and zero-ablating it changes the next-token distribution only weakly (KL ~1e-5), so the claim is retrospective. It is near zero on 'the'/'some'/'his', on 'a' in copular predicate nominatives ('she is a doctor'), on quantifier heads (few, number, lot, variety), and on degree words outside an indefinite phrase ('the range is very wide' is silent, 'the wide range' about half as strong).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Coastal cities around the world are confronting the consequences of rising sea levels, and planners are being forced to reconsider assumptions that once seemed secure. In the decades after the Second World War, many ports expanded rapidly, dredging channels and building warehouses along low-lying shorelines. The economic logic was straightforward: water offered transport, trade and tourism, and the land closest to it was cheap. Today, however, those same districts face chronic flooding, saltwater intrusion into drinking-water supplies and insurance premiums that climb faster than municipal budgets can absorb. Engineers have proposed sea walls, restored wetlands and floating neighborhoods, but each option carries costs that fall unevenly on residents. Wealthier homeowners can relocate inland; renters and small businesses often cannot. City councils, meanwhile, must balance the demands of developers against the warnings of scientists, and the political arithmetic rarely favors long-term spending over short-term growth. International bodies have begun to publish guidance, yet the recommendations remain broad and the financing scarce. Researchers at several universities have compiled a vast array of case studies documenting how communities adapt, from Rotterdam's storm-surge barriers to the mangrove restoration projects along the coast of Vietnam. What emerges from these accounts is not a single template but a set of principles: plan for the worst case, involve residents early, and treat infrastructure as a living system rather than a one-time construction project. One instructive case is the port of Marren, where a recent assessment concluded that nearly a third of the waterfront would be uninhabitable within thirty years under a mid-range emissions scenario. The report, commissioned after a storm surge destroyed two dozen blocks, recommended a managed retreat: buy out the most exposed properties, convert them to parkland and rebuild the harbor behind a raised levee. Business groups objected, arguing that the plan would erase jobs, while neighborhood associations complained they had been consulted only after the maps were drawn. A compromise eventually emerged, and construction began last spring. Whether the project succeeds will depend less on engineering than on trust, the report's authors concluded, and on whether the city can sustain funding across changes in administration. The next decade will test whether governments can translate those principles into action before the next major storm makes the question moot.
